title: Chapter 11 — Of the Extent of the Legislative Power
paragraphs: The great end of men’s entering into society is the enjoyment of their properties in peace and safety, and the great instrument and means of that is the laws established in that society. So the first and fundamental positive law of all commonwealths is the establishing of the legislative power — just as the first and fundamental natural law, which is to govern even the legislative itself, is the preservation of the society and (as far as is consistent with the public good) of every person in it. This legislative is not only the supreme power of the commonwealth, but sacred and unalterable in the hands where the community have once placed it. Nor can any edict of anyone else, in whatever form it is conceived or by whatever power it is backed, have the force and obligation of a law, if it does not have its sanction from the legislative which the public has chosen and appointed. For without this the law could not have what is absolutely necessary to its being a law:* the consent of the society, over which nobody can have a power to make laws except by their own consent and by authority received from them. And therefore all the obedience that anyone can be obliged to pay, even by the most solemn ties, ultimately ends in this supreme power and is directed by the laws it enacts. Nor can any oaths to any foreign power whatever, or to any subordinate power at home, release any member of the society from his obedience to the legislative when it acts in accordance with its trust; nor can they oblige him to any obedience contrary to the laws so enacted, or beyond what those laws allow. For it is ridiculous to imagine that anyone can be bound ultimately to obey any power in the society which is not the supreme.

(*“The lawful power of making laws to command whole political societies of men belongs so properly to those same entire societies that for any prince or potentate of any kind whatever on earth to exercise it by himself — and not by express commission immediately and personally received from God, or else by authority derived at first from the consent of those on whose persons they impose laws — is no better than mere tyranny. Laws, therefore, they are not, which public approval has not made so.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.

“On this point, therefore, we are to note that since men naturally have no full and perfect power to command whole political multitudes of men, it follows that utterly without our consent we could not in that way be at the command of any man living. And we do consent to be commanded when the society of which we are a part has at any time before consented, without afterwards revoking it by a like universal agreement. Human laws, therefore, of whatever kind, are valid by consent.” Ibid.)
Though the legislative — whether it is placed in one person or in more, and whether it is always in being or only at intervals — is the supreme power in every commonwealth, yet:

First, it is not, and cannot possibly be, absolutely arbitrary over the lives and fortunes of the people. For it is only the joint power of every member of the society, given up to the person or assembly that is legislator, and so it can be no more than those persons had in a state of nature before they entered into society and gave it up to the community. Nobody can transfer to another more power than he has in himself; and nobody has an absolute arbitrary power over himself, or over any other, to destroy his own life or to take away the life or property of another. A man, as has been proved, cannot subject himself to the arbitrary power of another. And since in the state of nature he has no arbitrary power over the life, liberty or possessions of another, but only as much as the law of nature gave him for the preservation of himself and the rest of mankind, this is all he does or can give up to the commonwealth, and through it to the legislative power. So the legislative can have no more than this. Their power, at its utmost bounds, is limited to the public good of the society. It is a power that has no other end but preservation, and therefore it can never have a right to destroy, enslave, or deliberately impoverish the subjects.* The obligations of the law of nature do not cease in society; in many cases they are only drawn closer, and human laws attach known penalties to them to enforce their observance. So the law of nature stands as an eternal rule to all men, legislators as well as others. The rules they make for other men’s actions must, like their own actions and other men’s, conform to the law of nature — that is, to the will of God, of which it is a declaration. And since the fundamental law of nature is the preservation of mankind, no human sanction can be good or valid against it.

(*“There are two foundations which bear up public societies: the one, a natural inclination, by which all men desire a sociable life and fellowship; the other, an order, expressly or secretly agreed on, concerning the manner of their union in living together. The latter is what we call the law of a commonwealth, the very soul of a political body, whose parts are given life by law, held together, and set to work in such actions as the common good requires. Political laws, ordained for outward order and government among men, are never framed as they should be unless they presume that the will of man is inwardly obstinate, rebellious, and averse to all obedience to the sacred laws of his nature. In a word, unless they presume that man, in respect of his depraved mind, is little better than a wild beast, and nevertheless provide accordingly to frame his outward actions so that they are no hindrance to the common good for which societies are instituted — unless they do this, they are not perfect.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

Secondly, the legislative, or supreme authority, cannot take to itself a power to rule by improvised, arbitrary decrees. It is bound to dispense justice and decide the rights of the subject by promulgated standing laws and known, authorized judges.* For the law of nature is unwritten, and so is nowhere to be found except in the minds of men. So those who, through passion or interest, misquote or misapply it cannot so easily be convinced of their mistake where there is no established judge. In that case it does not serve, as it ought, to determine the rights and fence in the properties of those who live under it — especially where everyone is judge, interpreter and executioner of it too, and that in his own case. And he who has right on his side ordinarily has only his own single strength, and so does not have force enough to defend himself from injuries or to punish offenders. To avoid these inconveniences, which disorder men’s properties in the state of nature, men unite into societies, so that they may have the united strength of the whole society to secure and defend their properties, and may have standing rules to set its bounds, by which everyone may know what is his. It is for this purpose that men give up all their natural power to the society they enter, and that the community puts the legislative power into such hands as they think fit — with this trust, that they shall be governed by declared laws. Otherwise their peace, quiet and property will still be as uncertain as they were in the state of nature.

(*“Human laws are measures in respect of men whose actions they must direct; yet they are such measures as also have their higher rules to be measured by. These rules are two: the law of God and the law of nature. So human laws must be made according to the general laws of nature, and without contradicting any positive law of Scripture; otherwise they are badly made.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book III, section 9.
“To force men to do anything inconvenient does seem unreasonable.” Ibid., book I, section 10.)

Absolute arbitrary power, and governing without settled standing laws, are neither of them consistent with the ends of society and government. Men would not give up the freedom of the state of nature for these ends, and bind themselves under government, were it not to preserve their lives, liberties and fortunes, and to secure their peace and quiet by stated rules of right and property. It cannot be supposed that they would intend, even if they had the power to do so, to give anyone, one or more, an absolute arbitrary power over their persons and estates, and to put a force into the magistrate’s hand to carry out his unlimited will arbitrarily upon them. That would be to put themselves into a worse condition than the state of nature, in which they had a liberty to defend their right against the injuries of others, and were on equal terms of force to maintain it, whether it was invaded by a single man or by many in combination. Whereas, if we suppose they have given themselves up to the absolute arbitrary power and will of a legislator, they have disarmed themselves and armed him, to make a prey of them whenever he pleases. For a man who is exposed to the arbitrary power of one man who commands 100,000 is in a much worse condition than one who is exposed to the arbitrary power of 100,000 separate men. Nobody can be sure that the will of the man who has such command is better than that of other men, though his force is 100,000 times stronger. And therefore, whatever form the commonwealth is under, the ruling power ought to govern by declared and received laws, and not by improvised dictates and undetermined resolutions. For mankind will be in a far worse condition than in the state of nature if they have armed one man, or a few, with the joint power of a multitude, to force them to obey at pleasure the exorbitant and unlimited decrees of their sudden thoughts, or their unrestrained and, until that moment, unknown wills, without any measures set down which may guide and justify their actions. For all the power the government has is only for the good of the society. So, just as it ought not to be arbitrary and at pleasure, it ought to be exercised by established and promulgated laws. In that way the people may know their duty and be safe and secure within the limits of the law; and the rulers too may be kept within their bounds, and not be tempted, by the power they have in their hands, to use it for such purposes, and by such measures, as they would not have known and would not willingly own.

Thirdly, the supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent. For the preservation of property is the end of government, and that for which men enter into society. This necessarily supposes and requires that the people should have property; otherwise they must be supposed to lose, by entering into society, the very thing that was the end for which they entered into it — too gross an absurdity for any man to accept. Men in society, therefore, having property, have such a right to the goods which by the law of the community are theirs that nobody has a right to take their substance, or any part of it, from them without their own consent. Without this they have no property at all. For I truly have no property in what another can by right take from me whenever he pleases, against my consent. So it is a mistake to think that the supreme or legislative power of any commonwealth can do what it will, and dispose of the estates of the subject arbitrarily, or take any part of them at pleasure. This is not much to be feared in governments where the legislative consists, wholly or in part, of assemblies which change, whose members, when the assembly is dissolved, are subjects under the common laws of their country, equally with the rest. But in governments where the legislative is one lasting assembly always in being, or one man, as in absolute monarchies, there is still a danger that they will think they have an interest distinct from the rest of the community, and so will be inclined to increase their own riches and power by taking what they think fit from the people. For a man’s property is not at all secure, even though there are good and fair laws to set its bounds between him and his fellow subjects, if the one who commands those subjects has power to take from any private man whatever part of his property he pleases, and to use and dispose of it as he thinks good.

But government, into whatever hands it is put, is entrusted, as I have shown before, on this condition and for this end: that men might have and secure their properties. So the prince or senate, however much power it may have to make laws for regulating property among the subjects, can never have a power to take to itself the whole, or any part, of the subjects’ property without their own consent; for this would in effect leave them no property at all. And to see that even absolute power, where it is necessary, is not arbitrary just because it is absolute, but is still limited by the reason, and confined to the ends, that required it to be absolute in some cases, we need look no further than the common practice of military discipline. The preservation of the army, and through it of the whole commonwealth, requires absolute obedience to the command of every superior officer, and it is justly death to disobey or dispute even the most dangerous or unreasonable of their commands. Yet we see that the sergeant, who could command a soldier to march up to the mouth of a cannon, or to stand in a breach where he is almost sure to die, cannot command that soldier to give him one penny of his money. Nor can the general, who can condemn him to death for deserting his post or for not obeying the most desperate orders, dispose of one farthing of that soldier’s estate, or seize one jot of his goods, with all his absolute power of life and death — though he can command him to do anything, and hang him for the least disobedience. For such blind obedience is necessary to the end for which the commander has his power, namely the preservation of the rest; but disposing of the soldier’s goods has nothing to do with that end.

It is true that governments cannot be supported without great expense, and it is right that everyone who enjoys his share of the protection should pay his proportion toward its maintenance out of his estate. But it must still be with his own consent — that is, the consent of the majority, given either by themselves or by representatives they have chosen. For if anyone claims a power to lay and levy taxes on the people by his own authority, and without such consent of the people, he thereby invades the fundamental law of property and subverts the end of government. For what property have I in something that another may by right take for himself whenever he pleases?

Fourthly, the legislative cannot transfer the power of making laws to any other hands. For since it is only a power delegated from the people, those who have it cannot pass it over to others. The people alone can appoint the form of the commonwealth, which they do by constituting the legislative and appointing in whose hands it shall be. And when the people have said, “We will submit to rules and be governed by laws made by such men, and in such forms,” nobody else can say that other men shall make laws for them. Nor can the people be bound by any laws except those enacted by the men they have chosen and authorized to make laws for them. The power of the legislative is derived from the people by a positive, voluntary grant and institution, and so it can be no other than what that positive grant conveyed. That grant was only to make laws, not to make legislators. So the legislative can have no power to transfer its authority of making laws and place it in other hands.

These, then, are the bounds that the trust placed in them by the society, together with the law of God and of nature, have set to the legislative power of every commonwealth, under all forms of government.

First, they are to govern by promulgated, established laws, which are not to be varied in particular cases, but are to have one rule for rich and poor, for the favourite at court and the countryman at the plough.
Secondly, these laws ought also to be designed, ultimately, for no other end than the good of the people.

Thirdly, they must not raise taxes on the property of the people without the consent of the people, given by themselves or by their deputies. And strictly speaking, this concerns only governments where the legislative is always in being, or at least where the people have not reserved any part of the legislative to deputies whom they themselves choose from time to time.
Fourthly, the legislative neither must nor can transfer the power of making laws to anybody else, or place it anywhere but where the people have placed it.
